clue.text: Inverted section of Sugarloaf is same as mountainous rock

indicators.note: Inverted says the hidden letters are read backwards
section of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A geological remark comparing part of Rio's Sugarloaf Mountain to other mountain rock.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition took in 'as', but 'as mountainous rock' cannot stand in for a noun; 'as' is a link and 'mountainous rock' alone is the definition. 'Inverted' turns FISSAM round.
explanation.definitionFit: A massif is a compact mass of mountains, a block of upland rock.

clue.text: Existential question from Spanish hero forgetting theory primarily essential for life?

indicators.note: forgetting tells us to drop a letter from the question that comes before it

parts.note: 'Am I not?' is a question about whether one exists at all

indicators.note: primarily means take only the first letter of the word theory

parts.note: a Cid: El Cid is the medieval Spanish hero, so a Spanish hero is 'a Cid'

explanation.surface: A Spanish hero, minus his theory, wonders about his existence while hinting at what life needs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forgetting' removes T (the first letter of 'theory', signalled by 'primarily') from AM I NOT, leaving AMINO; 'from' is a link. The question mark marks the definition as a loose description rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, and some must be eaten because living things cannot do without them.

clue.text: Meek followers of singular slimy law clerk

parts.note: S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular
Uriah Heep is the oily, fawning lawyer's clerk in Dickens's David Copperfield

explanation.surface: Timid underlings trailing after one particularly greasy solicitor's clerk.
explanation.walkthrough: Uriah Heep, from Dickens's novel David Copperfield, is famous for being 'ever so humble' and slimy.
explanation.definitionFit: People who follow along meekly without thinking are called a flock of these docile farm animals.

clue.text: Close feature destroyed, a canal, tit for tat

indicators.note: something destroyed is broken apart, so these letters are torn up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A neighbourhood feature wrecked along with a canal, in an exchange of retaliation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close' looks like a street or cul-de-sac, but it is the actress Glenn Close, and a 'feature' is a feature film. 'Destroyed' rearranges A CANAL TIT FOR TAT.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1987 thriller starring Glenn Close is a feature film in which she plays the obsessive lover.

clue.text: Intensify repulsing of pawns after dismissing middle one

indicators.note: dismissing middle one tells us to remove the central letter of the reversed word
repulsing means driving back, so the word for pawns is read backwards

parts.note: pawns are people used by others, i.e. puppets

explanation.surface: A chess player steps up the pressure by driving back pawns, losing the central one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repulsing of' turns PUPPETS into STEPPUP; 'dismissing middle one' drops its fourth letter, P, of seven. 'After' is a link. Chess suggests pawns are pieces, but here they are puppets.
explanation.definitionFit: To step something up is to increase or escalate it.

clue.text: Man held by nurse, frequently a role model? Notice there's no getting past it

indicators.note: held by means the word for man sits inside the word for nurse

parts.note: to nurse is to tend
a man is referred to as he
oft is an old word for often, frequently
a hero is someone looked up to as a role model
a notice in a paper is an ad, an advertisement

explanation.surface: A nurse looking after a man often serves as an example, though a sign warns the way ahead is blocked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Held by' signals a container; 'a' before 'role model' is a link word. The definition is the second sentence: a point beyond which no one can go.
explanation.definitionFit: A dead end or final point is a place beyond which nobody can travel or progress.

clue.text: See gathering of fabric in lifted upper garment, casual one

indicators.note: in means the following pieces are placed inside the reversed garment word
lifted in a down clue means the word is read upwards, i.e. backwards

parts.note: a top is an upper garment
lo is an old word for look, see
shir, also spelt shirr, is a gathering of fabric made with parallel rows of stitches

explanation.surface: Look at the ruched cloth in this raised top, a relaxed item of clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifted' reverses in a down clue, and 'in' signals a container. SHIR is a less common spelling of shirr. 'Casual one' means a casual upper garment, echoing 'upper garment' earlier.
explanation.definitionFit: A short-sleeved collared knit top is standard informal wear.

clue.text: Played away, keeping as well as one with perilously low sex drive?

definitions.text: one with perilously low sex drive?

indicators.note: keeping means the first pair of letters holds the next piece inside

parts.note: P is the abbreviation for played in sports league tables
A is the abbreviation for away in sports fixtures
as well as means and

explanation.surface: Someone played away from home, and keeps a partner with a worryingly weak libido.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Played away' suggests infidelity, but it is just P and A from football league tables. Giant pandas are notoriously reluctant to breed in captivity, which endangers the species.
explanation.definitionFit: The bamboo-eating bear breeds so rarely that its numbers are in danger, a famously low reproductive urge.

clue.text: Crazy mother raised first son

parts.note: ma is a familiar word for mother

indicators.note: raised in a down clue means the word is read upwards, i.e. backwards

parts.note: Cain was the first son of Adam and Eve in Genesis

explanation.surface: A mad mother brings up her eldest boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised' looks like bringing up a child, but it turns CAIN upwards to NIAC.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as an adjective, the word describes wild, frenzied, unhinged behaviour.

clue.text: The logical response to sales resistance?

definitions.text: The logical response to sales resistance?

parts.words: The logical response to sales resistance?
parts.note: in physics, resistance to change in motion has a name; the clue jokes that a selling technique relying on customers doing nothing is the natural answer to buyers who resist

explanation.surface: A marketing question about how to overcome customers who won't buy.
explanation.walkthrough: The practice is sending unrequested goods and charging if the recipient does not return them, so it exploits the buyer's passivity; physics' 'resistance' to motion supplies the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: This illegal sales practice relies on people's passivity, the physics term for a body's resistance to change.

clue.text: Polonium's decayed after constant pressure

indicators.note: after means the anagram comes behind the constant

parts.note: c is the symbol for a constant, e.g. the speed of light

indicators.note: radioactive elements decay, breaking down into other forms, so these letters are reformed

parts.note: the letters of polonium plus the s of the possessive

explanation.surface: A radioactive element has broken down after being kept under steady force.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decayed' suits polonium, a radioactive element, and is the anagram signal; here the 's of the possessive supplies a real letter. C for a constant is a physics convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Being under pressure to do something is a strong urging or force driving one to act.

clue.text: Backing waterproofs skin or fleece

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the word for waterproofs is reversed

parts.note: macs, short for mackintoshes, are waterproof raincoats

explanation.surface: Waterproof coats with a backing of animal skin or sheep's wool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skin' and 'fleece' look like coat linings, but both are verbs meaning to swindle.
explanation.definitionFit: To skin or fleece someone is to cheat them out of money, a swindle.

clue.text: Small share of profits keeps long-playing cast, say

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

indicators.note: keeps means the share word holds the next piece inside it

parts.note: a cut is a share of the takings
LP stands for long-playing record

explanation.surface: A small cut of the profits pays for a long-running cast, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long-playing cast' suggests a theatre company, but 'cast, say' is the definition: casting metal or plaster is one way of making a sculpture.
explanation.definitionFit: Casting in bronze is one example of shaping a figure in three dimensions.

clue.text: Train mole? He could better that!

definitions.text: Train mole? He could better that!

indicators.note: could better means could improve on, here rearranging the letters into a better order

explanation.surface: Training a mole? Someone else could outdo that feat!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Could better' rearranges TRAIN MOLE; read whole, the clue says a man who trains lions does something more impressive than training a mole.
explanation.definitionFit: A circus performer who trains big cats does a far braver job than schooling a small burrowing animal.

clue.text: Unenthusiastic, chilling cabinet barring French president

parts.note: a cool response is an unenthusiastic one

indicators.note: barring means excluding, so the abbreviation is taken out

parts.note: a fridge is a cabinet for chilling food

explanation.surface: A lukewarm cabinet keeps the French head of state out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French president' looks like one phrase, but 'French' gives FR, removed by 'barring', and 'president' alone is the definition: Calvin Coolidge was US president 1923-29.
explanation.definitionFit: Calvin Coolidge was the thirtieth head of state of the United States.

clue.text: Level of martial skill on which one can't build much

definitions.meaning: in judo and karate a coloured belt marks a grade of skill

definitions.text: on which one can't build much
definitions.meaning: protected countryside around a town where development is restricted

explanation.surface: A karate grade compared to land where construction is banned.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the British planning term for a protected ring of open land around a city.
explanation.definitionFit: A coloured judo belt marks an intermediate grade, while the planning term names countryside protected from housing development.

clue.text: With this a language may be written or imaged, possibly

definitions.text: With this a language may be written or imaged, possibly

indicators.note: possibly means the letters could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A remark about a script in which language is written or shown in pictures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges OR IMAGED; the whole clue also describes the answer, a picture-symbol script.
explanation.definitionFit: A pictographic symbol represents an idea directly, as in Chinese characters, so a language can be written in such signs.

clue.text: Fiddle and euphonium finally in tune?

indicators.note: finally means take only the last letter of euphonium

parts.note: on key means in tune

explanation.surface: A violin and a euphonium playing in tune together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiddle' looks like a violin, but is the verb: to monkey about is to fiddle or tamper. 'And' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To monkey with something is to tamper or meddle with it.

clue.text: Diminutive singer was first among peers, perhaps

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird
led means was first, at the front

explanation.surface: A small vocalist topped the charts among their equals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peers' looks like equals, but means members of the nobility. 'Perhaps' signals that holding a title is only one way of being a peer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lords and dukes hold an aristocratic rank, so a noble is someone with a title.

clue.text: Show disgust but not quite malice

indicators.note: not quite means the word is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: spite means malice

explanation.surface: Expressing revulsion that isn't quite spiteful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'But' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Expelling saliva is a traditional gesture of contempt.

clue.text: Who stole away with beauty from "gay" city?

definitions.meaning: the Trojan prince who carried off Helen, the most beautiful woman, sparking the Trojan War
the French capital is called Gay Paree, gay in its old sense of merry

explanation.surface: A question about a thief fleeing a lively city with a beautiful woman.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth the Trojan prince abducted Helen of Troy. 'Gay' is in quotes because the city's nickname uses its old meaning of merry.
explanation.definitionFit: The prince of Troy abducted Helen in myth, and the French capital shares his name.

clue.text: Familiar with reinterpretations of songs about northern worker, say

indicators.note: about means the song word goes around the next letter

parts.note: covers are new versions of songs by other artists
a worker ant is one type of ant, so worker suggests ant

explanation.surface: Someone familiar with cover versions of songs about a northern labourer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worker' suggests a labourer, but it is the worker ant, a crossword staple; 'say' flags it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Being conversant with a subject means knowing it well, being acquainted with it.

clue.text: Hold back page after cursory reading

indicators.note: after means the page abbreviation follows the reading word

parts.note: to skim is to read quickly and superficially

explanation.surface: Withholding a page after only glancing at it.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrimp or be stingy is to hold back on spending or effort.

clue.text: Where RAC runs in 4, exclusively, occasionally

definitions.meaning: in the answer to 4 down the letters RAC sit between two Ts, so they run from T to T, not counting those Ts; T stands for time

explanation.surface: A note on where a motoring organisation operates only now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: The RAC is the Royal Automobile Club, a British motoring organisation, but here it is just three letters within FATAL ATTRACTION. T is the physics symbol for time.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something at irregular intervals means doing it now and then.

clue.text: Draped garment of Mordor's Dark Lord abandoning universal good

indicators.note: abandoning means leaving behind, so the letter is dropped

parts.note: Sauron is the Dark Lord of Mordor in Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings
U is the film-classification abbreviation for universal

explanation.surface: Tolkien's villain gives up general goodness and is left with a wrap-around garment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abandoning' removes U (universal, the British film rating) from SAURON to give SARON; 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A length of cloth wrapped round the waist, worn in South-East Asia, is a draped item of clothing.

clue.text: Task involving something more than a single agent

indicators.note: involving means the task word wraps round the next piece

parts.note: a duty is a task
an EP, extended play, is a record with more tracks than a single

explanation.surface: A job demanding more than one solitary operative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Single' suggests a lone agent but is a single record; an EP is longer.
explanation.definitionFit: A deputy acts on another's behalf, a representative or stand-in.
